quotes_and_pages.verbatim_quote: It is important for proper subsurface correlations to understand that clino- forms, which represent geological time lines, crosscut lithostratigraphic boundaries. The hypothetical example in Fig. 9.10 shows correlations based upon lithofacies (stratigraphic intervals with similarities in well log response) and upon geological time. Note that shaley and heterolithic intervals separate sandy intervals, so that the sands between wells 1 and 2 are not in communi- cation. This feature will adversely affect waterflood performance as well as single-well productivity. A similar example is presented for the modern Mekong River Delta in Fig. 9.11 (after Gani and Bhattacharya, 2005). Progradation of the delta has been age-dated for the last 6000 years. Lithostratigraphic and sequence strati- graphic (chronostratigraphic) correlations are given to illustrate the crossing nature of time lines and lithofacies boundaries. The true chronostratigraphic correlations demonstrate the potential for lateral discontinuities within the lithostratigraphic intervals. In addition to sea-level fluctuations, deltas are subject to “delta distribu- tary switching processes,” such as modeled in Fig. 9.12. According to Overeem et al. (2005), channel switching may be an even more important control on the evolution of deltaic systems than is sea-level change. Deltas can also form during a relative fall in sea level; these are often referred to as “lowstand” or “shelf-margin” deltas or systems tracts (Figs. 5.18 and 5.19). These deposits form in response to early fall in sea level, which causes valley incision, and a seaward retreat and lowering of the shoreline. Although important, these lowstand deltas are generally not as large, nor as prevalent as highstand deltas.

quotes_and_pages.verbatim_quote: 9.4 RIVER-DOMINATED DELTA DEPOSITS AND RESERVOIRS 9.4.1 Processes and Deposits The Mississippi River Delta (Fig. 9.13) has long been considered the “type” river-dominated delta (Fig. 9.5). Strong waves and currents do not impinge upon its protected shoreline, so sediment deposited at and near the shore zone is not reworked or dispersed laterally (Figs. 9.4 and 9.7). With time and suf- ficient accommodation space between the sea surface and seafloor to accept sediment, such a delta will prograde seaward (Fig. 9.9), as will the delta zones (Fig. 9.7). By that process, surfaces representing instants in geologic time crosscut boundaries between sedimentary facies (see the time lines or clino- forms in Fig. 9.9). However, over time, progradation and vertical aggradation lead to a progressive shallowing of the water depth, to the point at which the main river(s) feeding sediment to its delta will shift toward deeper water (toward lower points on the seafloor), thereby causing the distributary-channel switching discussed earlier (Fig. 9.11). During the past 4600 years, there have been no fewer than eight periods of channel and lobe switching on the Missis- sippi River Delta (Fig. 9.12). The main facies of a river-dominated delta, and their distribution in space, are shown in Fig. 9.14. Sandy reservoir facies are deposits of distributary channels and distributary mouth-bars. quotes_and_pages.verbatim_quote: In Prudhoe Bay field, formative processes of distributary mouth bars were evaluated by Tye and Hickey (2001). A 1000-ft. (300-m) horizontal well was drilled into a distributary mouth-bar reservoir sandstone, and three cores were obtained. Seven sandy lithofacies were identified in the core, all are moderately to very well sorted and fine to very fine-grained. Six of the lithofacies exhibit average horizontal permeabilities of 12–40 md. The seventh, best-sorted lithofa- cies averages 129 md. The origin of these lithofacies was determined by study- ing modern river-dominated delta processes and sediments. Geoscientists believe that sediment plumes emanating from distributary channels during flood stage deposited the best-sorted and most-permeable sands (the seventh lithofa- cies) at the apex or most-proximal part of the distributary mouth bars, as well as along the proximal-bar margin (Fig. 9.16). Finer-grained, more poorly sorted sands and muds were deposited more distally, under lower flow-regime conditions.
